label: Brazil

governmentText.minority: {party} edges the runoff with {seats} points, short of a clear mandate.
governmentText.hung: Dead heat. The electoral court counts through the night, and the country waits.

goalHint: Win {majority} of {total} presidency points. The first round is already counted: the opening map includes the voters of the eliminated candidates, and the campaign events show them moving. National broadcasts and platform preparation reach the whole electorate.

issues.name: Jobs and inflation
issues.blurb: Prices at the market, wages at the end of the month and whether the factory is hiring.

issues.name: Bolsa Familia and social programmes
issues.blurb: Cash transfers, the minimum wage and who gets to keep them.

issues.name: Corruption
issues.blurb: From the mensalao to Lava Jato: who stole, who got caught and who got off.

issues.name: Crime and security
issues.blurb: Homicides, militias, prisons and the police.

issues.name: Family, faith and values
issues.blurb: Abortion, schools and the evangelical churches' role in politics.

issues.name: Democracy and institutions
issues.blurb: Whether the courts, the press and the voting machines are trusted.

issues.name: Amazon and environment
issues.blurb: Deforestation, farmland and Brazil's standing abroad.

issues.name: State companies and privatisation
issues.blurb: Petrobras, the banks and what the state should own.

issues.name: Public finances and the currency
issues.blurb: The deficit, the debt, the real and what the creditors think.

2002.label: 2002 · Lula v. Serra
2002.tagline: October 27, 2002. After three failed runs, Lula is 23 points clear of José Serra, the government's candidate. But the real is sliding, the IMF has lent 30 billion dollars, and the creditors are nervous. Hold the lead without frightening them, or make Brazil afraid of the leap.

events.headline: The first round: Lula 46.4 percent, twice Serra's 23.2. The polls call the runoff a formality, and {party} knows a formality can be lost
The real hits a record low against the dollar despite the IMF's 30 billion dollar package. The government that signed it owns the crisis, and {party} pays for it
Anthony Garotinho and Ciro Gomes both come out for Lula. The 30 percent of voters they shared in October lines up behind him, in Rio and in the Northeast
Bankers reread Lula's Letter to the Brazilian People: he will honour the contracts and the debt. The Duda Mendonça ads sell 'Lulinha paz e amor' to the voters who fear him
Serra leans on experience: the health minister who forced down the price of AIDS drugs and brought generics to the pharmacy. The pitch lands in the south and São Paulo
The last debate, on Globo two days out: Serra goes after Lula's preparation, and Lula stays calm and refuses the bait. The calm is the story
Serra keeps his distance from Fernando Henrique Cardoso, whose approval is low, and the government coalition grumbles. {party} fights without its own record
José Alencar, the textile employer on Lula's ticket, takes the case to boardrooms: a union man and a boss on one poster
Lula's Zero Hunger pledge, three meals a day for every Brazilian, fills his rallies in the Northeast, and {party} has the poorest towns
Gang violence in Rio and São Paulo dominates the evening news. The sitting government gets the blame, and security tops the list of voters' fears
{party}'s candidate wins the debate on Globo, and the clip is everywhere by morning

2006.label: 2006 · Lula v. Alckmin
2006.tagline: October 29, 2006. Lula survived the mensalão and the dossier scandal, missed an outright win by 1.4 points, and now meets Geraldo Alckmin in a runoff about corruption on one side and privatisation on the other. The poor North and East are with him. São Paulo is not.

events.headline: The first round: Lula 48.6, Alckmin 41.6, Heloísa Helena 6.9. A win that was sure a month ago slipped away in the last fortnight, and {party} calls it a reprieve
Federal police photograph almost two million reais in cash held by PT aides who were buying a dossier on PSDB candidates. The pictures are broadcast two days before the first round
PT ads say Alckmin will sell Petrobras, Banco do Brasil and the Caixa. The privatisation charge lands because he cannot shake his party's record
Alckmin pulls on a jacket covered in the logos of Petrobras, Banco do Brasil and the Caixa to swear he will sell none of them. The picture is mocked, and the denial still lands
Three years of Bolsa Familia, a rising minimum wage and cheap credit reach the poorest quarter of the country. In the Northeast the runoff is already decided
In the last debate, Alckmin presses on the mensalão and the dossier, Lula answers with the record of eight years of the PSDB. Neither lands a knockout
The mensalão, a cash-for-votes scheme in Congress, still hangs over the party's old guard. Voters who liked Lula's policies say they do not trust the PT
Heloísa Helena, the left-wing third-place finisher, keeps her distance from both finalists. Her 7 percent are the most volatile voters of the runoff
Alckmin stays on message in his home state, where he was governor, and the PSDB machine runs its best operation of the campaign. São Paulo stays the opposition's stronghold
Lula's rallies in the Northeast draw crowds that the first round never showed. {party} has the crowd and the momentum
{party}'s candidate wins the debate on Globo, and the clip is everywhere by morning

2010.label: 2010 · Rousseff v. Serra
2010.tagline: October 31, 2010. Lula leaves office with approval near 80 percent and hands the ticket to a chief of staff who has never won an election. Marina Silva's 20 million votes forced a second round, and the last three weeks turn on abortion and religion more than the economy.

events.headline: The first round: Rousseff 46.9, Serra 32.6, Marina Silva 19.3. Rousseff missed an outright win after a late slide over religion, and {party} has three weeks to reassemble the vote
Erenice Guerra, Rousseff's successor as chief of staff, had resigned over relatives' lobbying in September, and the story is back in the runoff. {party} is asked what she knew
Chain emails and church bulletins call Rousseff pro-abortion and anti-religion. Serra's side leans in, and abortion, not the economy, dominates the week
Rousseff issues a message to the people of God, promising not to change the abortion law and to respect every faith. It calms some pulpits, and not the loudest ones
Marina Silva's Green Party declares itself independent. She will ask for votes for neither finalist, and her 20 million voters are left to choose
Something hits Serra at a Rio rally, and he goes for a scan. The 'paper ball' becomes the joke of the week, and the TV cameras lose a day of his message
Lula goes on the road for Rousseff in every state and puts his approval on the ticket. {party} has the machine
Serra promises a minimum wage of 600 reais, well above the government's figure. It is a bid for the poor, but not his record
The economy grows at close to 7 percent and unemployment sits at a record low. The incumbent party takes credit, and {party} owns the mood
Serra's home state of São Paulo is his firewall, and the opposition's best result comes in its suburbs. Whether it is enough is the question of the campaign
{party}'s candidate wins the debate on Globo, and the clip is everywhere by morning

2014.label: 2014 · Rousseff v. Neves
2014.tagline: October 26, 2014. Marina Silva surged past Rousseff in runoff polls for weeks after Eduardo Campos died in a plane crash, until the PT's advertising and Aécio Neves's late climb pushed her to third. Now the PT's fourth term is on the line: slow growth, the Petrobras investigation, and a country that votes by region.

events.headline: The first round: Rousseff 41.6, Neves 33.6, Marina Silva 21.3. Silva's collapse hands the runoff to a fight between the PT and the PSDB, and {party} wakes up in a new race
Marina Silva and her party, the PSB, back Aécio Neves, despite a campaign in which his side pounded her. The 22 million who voted for her are courted by both camps
PT ads warn that the opposition would cut Bolsa Familia and workers' rights. In the Northeast, it works as designed

Testimony from a former Petrobras director's plea deal, leaked since September, keeps a scheme of kickbacks on refinery contracts, tied to the ruling coalition, in the news. The scandal gets a name, the petrolão
In the final TV debate, Aécio presses the economy and the scandal, and Rousseff presses the record of the PSDB governments. Both claim the night

Two days out, a news magazine puts a witness's claim on its cover that Lula and Rousseff knew of the Petrobras scheme. Rousseff's team calls it electoral terrorism, and the story dominates the last weekend
Growth stays flat and inflation sits at the top of the target band. The government's 'we are creating jobs' line runs into the supermarket receipts
Social media splits the map: the Northeast posts for Rousseff, the South and São Paulo for Neves, and the insults travel both ways. Turnout rises on both sides
Neves campaigns for his home state, where he was governor for eight years. Minas Gerais still tilts to Rousseff, and {party} has to explain the Mineiro vote
A July report that a Minas Gerais airport was built with state money on land that belonged to Neves's great-uncle while he was governor resurfaces. {party} spends a news cycle answering
{party}'s candidate wins the debate on Globo, and the clip is everywhere by morning

2018.label: 2018 · Haddad v. Bolsonaro
2018.tagline: October 28, 2018. Lula is in prison and barred, his stand-in has had seven weeks to introduce himself, and the front-runner was stabbed in a crowd and has skipped every debate since. Fear of the PT and fear of Bolsonaro are both at record highs. Ciro Gomes holds 13 million votes and has flown to Europe.

events.headline: The first round: Bolsonaro 46 percent, a hair short of winning outright, Haddad 29. The PT has to turn a 17-point gap into a campaign

'Ele não': the women's protests that filled squares in dozens of cities before the first round stay at the centre of the runoff. The slogan trends everywhere, but Bolsonaro's numbers among women barely move
Ciro Gomes leaves for Europe after the first round and does not take the stage with Haddad. His 13 million voters are left to decide for themselves
A newspaper reports that businessmen are paying for mass WhatsApp messages against the PT. The electoral court agrees to look into it, and the chains keep spreading
Bolsonaro skips every runoff debate on medical advice. Haddad faces an empty chair and a clock running out
Bolsonaro addresses the Avenida Paulista rally by video from his home, promising to 'sweep the red bandits' out of Brazil. The words travel further than the crowd
The 'gay kit' claim, a false story about a school textbook, reaches every church group in the country. {party} has no answer that fits on a phone screen
Paulo Guedes, Bolsonaro's economist, promises privatisations and a flat tax. Investors cheer, and workers hear the word cuts
A video resurfaces of Eduardo Bolsonaro saying it would take 'a soldier and a corporal' to shut the Supreme Court. Democracy becomes a ballot question, and {party} gets the benefit
Lula's face is still on every PT poster, from his cell in Curitiba. 'Haddad is Lula' holds the base and scares everyone else
The knife attack in Juiz de Fora is replayed again, and the sympathy bounce for {party} never quite goes away
{party}'s candidate wins the debate on Globo, and the clip is everywhere by morning

2022.label: 2022 · Lula v. Bolsonaro
2022.tagline: October 30, 2022. A former president whose convictions were annulled against an incumbent who spent the year doubting the voting machines. Lula led the first round by five points and the polls missed Bolsonaro's strength. Minas Gerais, a record Northeast turnout and the 7 percent who backed Tebet or Ciro Gomes decide it.

events.headline: The first round: Lula 48.4, Bolsonaro 43.2, and the pollsters undercounted the incumbent by several points. {party} learns the gap is not a lead
Simone Tebet, third with 4 percent, backs Lula and takes to the road for him. Moderate, centre-right voters in São Paulo and Mato Grosso do Sul are the target
Auxílio Brasil is raised to 600 reais months before the vote, and the state pays out in the final weeks. {party} gets a hearing in the poorest towns
Bolsonaro tells a podcast that 'a mood came up' when he met teenage Venezuelan girls in a Brasília suburb. Women voters, his weakest group, hear it, and {party} pays
Roberto Jefferson, a Bolsonaro ally, fires on federal police sent to arrest him. The campaign spends its last week explaining it
Election day: police roadblocks on Northeast highways slow buses to the polling stations. Turnout there comes in high anyway, and {party} gets the benefit
Minas Gerais governor Romeu Zema backs Bolsonaro and both campaigns camp in Belo Horizonte. The state that picks the winner gets a visit a week
Lula's promise of beef and a beer on the weekend lands in the supermarket aisles, and {party} owns the cost of living
Rumours that Lula will close churches run through pastors' WhatsApp groups. Lula answers with a letter to evangelicals, and {party} has to defend its faith record
Bolsonaro's team plays back the Lava Jato years in every ad break, and {party} spends the week on the corruption question
The 7 percent who backed Tebet or Ciro Gomes are the only voters left to win, and both campaigns flood them with ads
{party}'s candidate wins the debate on Globo, and the clip is everywhere by morning
A fresh Datafolha poll shows {party} gaining among undecided voters
A viral WhatsApp chain, true or not, spreads faster than the campaign can answer, and {party} takes the hit
A popular governor lends {party} his machine and his rallies for the final stretch
Evangelical pastors, some with their own television stations, back {party} from the pulpit
A Northeast turnout drive fills the buses to the polling stations, and {party} benefits
Farm leaders fill a rally in the interior and lean on {party}'s side of the ticket
A leaked police report puts a campaign ally in the headlines, and {party} loses a news cycle
The monthly inflation number comes in hot, and the incumbent pays for it
A packed rally in São Paulo electrifies {party}
{party}'s free television hour lands, and the jingle is on every radio
The networks offer {party} a head-to-head debate slot
events.prompt: A head-to-head is on the table. How do you play it?

choices.text: Accept and go on the attack
choices.resultText: You land blows and take a few. The overnight polls twitch your way.
A steady, on-message night. No gaffes, no fireworks.

choices.text: Decline: protect the lead and avoid the ambush
choices.resultText: You dodge the studio lights. The press calls it a hiding.

events.headline: The third-place finisher holds millions of votes and has not said who to back
events.prompt: The voters of the candidate who finished third will decide the runoff. What do you offer?

choices.text: A written policy deal, with commitments you can be held to
choices.resultText: The camp declares for you, grudgingly. Your base wonders what you gave away.

choices.text: Skip the leader and court the voters directly with targeted ads
choices.resultText: Some come over. Without an endorsement, many stay home.

choices.text: Ignore the courting: run to your own base
choices.resultText: Your base turns out. The third camp drifts toward your rival or stays at home.

events.headline: The centrão parties offer {party} their support, for a price
events.prompt: The big, shifting block of centre parties wants ministries and budget amendments. What do you do?

choices.text: Take the deal: their machines and airtime for ministries
choices.resultText: The mayors and radio stations switch to you. The press runs a week of stories about the price.

choices.text: Refuse and campaign on a clean slate
choices.resultText: Clean hands, thinner machine. The base cheers and the interior goes quiet.

choices.text: Refuse, and attack the rival for taking the same deal
choices.resultText: You define them more than yourself, and it lands.

events.headline: {party}'s programme committee is split on the big pledge
events.prompt: The draft is ready. Which way do you push?

choices.text: Go bold with a defining, risky pledge
choices.resultText: The base roars. The spreadsheets at HQ look nervous.

choices.text: Play it cautious: no hostages to fortune
Make it a contrast document against the rival
choices.resultText: You define them more than yourself, and it lands.
